titre: Inge Lehmann, the Core Hidden Inside the Core
accroche: In 1929, European seismographs pick up waves where theory says there should be nothing. A Danish seismologist sees a core within the core.
contenu_vulgarise:
On June 17, 1929, a magnitude 7.3 earthquake shakes Murchison, New Zealand, almost exactly on the opposite side of the globe from Denmark. In Copenhagen, the seismologist Inge Lehmann has been running the seismology department of the Royal Danish Geodetic Institute for a year. Going through the recordings of this earthquake and others like it, she notices an anomaly that the prevailing theory does not predict: faint compression waves, known as P waves, show up where they simply should not be detectable.

## A Shadow That Lets a Little Light Through

An earthquake sends two main types of waves through the globe: P waves, which pass through solids and liquids alike, and S waves, which do not pass through liquids. By the early 20th century, seismologists already know, from the disappearance of S waves beyond 104° from the epicenter, that the center of the Earth is liquid, at least in part. This liquid core also bends P waves as they pass through it, which creates a shadow zone, between 104° and 140°, where no direct wave should reach the surface, in the same way that an opaque obstacle casts a sharp shadow behind a light source. Yet, in this shadow zone, seismographs still record faint P waves.

Lehmann proposes an explanation: at the center of the liquid core there would be a second, deeper boundary, separating off an inner core in which waves travel faster. This boundary would send some of the waves back toward the shadow zone, like a second obstacle placed behind the first. She publishes the hypothesis in 1936, in a twenty-nine-page paper soberly titled “P',” after the name she gives to these waves reflected by the inner boundary.

## Thirty-Five Years to Confirm a Shadow

The hypothesis remains one interpretation among others for decades: no instrument of the time can directly decide between a solid inner core and a mere continuous variation in density. It takes until 1971 for calculations to confirm, from the same bent waves, the existence of a sharp boundary between the inner core and the outer core. That is the same year Lehmann becomes the first woman to receive the William Bowie Medal, the highest honor in American geophysics, for a career carried out from a country with no deep ocean or active volcano, using nothing but the traces of a seismograph.

She keeps publishing until 1987, when her last paper appears, at age 99, and dies in Copenhagen in 1993, at 104. In 1995, the American Geophysical Union creates an annual medal in her name, awarded to those who advance the understanding of the Earth's mantle and core. An institutional recognition that comes after her, but that extends what her career had already shown: one can read the deep structure of a planet without ever descending into it, as long as one takes seriously a shadow that should let no light through.

citation.texte: We take it that, as before, the Earth consists of a core and a mantle, but that inside the core there is an inner core in which the velocity is larger than in the outer one.

carte.punch: She saw a core inside the core, without ever going down there.
carte.idee: In 1936, the Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann spots faint seismic waves where theory says there should be nothing. She deduces the existence of a second, solid core, hidden at the center of the Earth's liquid core. Calculations would confirm it thirty-five years later.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Details of the New Zealand earthquake whose analysis put Lehmann on the trail of the inner core, from New Zealand's official geological agency.

quiz.question: Why did the faint P waves detected in the seismic “shadow zone” after the 1929 earthquake put Inge Lehmann on the trail of a second core?
choix: Because the European seismographs of the time were faulty and recorded phantom waves
Because these waves actually came from a second earthquake occurring at the same moment elsewhere in the Pacific
Because a single liquid core is not enough to explain their presence: an additional internal boundary was needed to send them back to the surface
Because the shadow zone concerns only S waves, so the waves detected must have been misidentified S waves
quiz.explication: The shadow zone, between 104° and 140°, exists because the liquid core bends P waves and stops S waves. A liquid core alone, with no internal structure, sends no waves into this zone: the presence of faint P waves therefore required a second, deeper boundary capable of reflecting them. Neither an instrument fault nor a second earthquake could have produced a signal this consistent from station to station.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is already known, in the early 20th century, about the disappearance of S waves beyond 104° from an earthquake's epicenter?
choix: That it proves the existence of a solid inner core distinct from the outer core
That it proves the center of the Earth is liquid, at least in part
That it is due to a sensitivity flaw in the seismographs of the time
That it concerns only earthquakes occurring in the Southern Hemisphere
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is this disappearance of S waves, which do not pass through liquids, that establishes at the start of the century that part of the Earth's center is liquid, even before Lehmann's hypothesis of a second core.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happens in 1971, the year Inge Lehmann receives the William Bowie Medal?
choix: Calculations confirm the existence of a sharp boundary between the inner and outer core
A new earthquake on the opposite side of the globe from Denmark provides the first data of its kind
Lehmann publishes her hypothesis of a second core for the first time
The American Geophysical Union creates an annual medal in her name
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 1936 hypothesis remained one interpretation among others; it is calculations published in 1971 that finally confirm a sharp boundary, the same year as her William Bowie Medal.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the card, what makes Inge Lehmann's career remarkable from a geographic standpoint?
choix: It took place entirely in New Zealand, near the epicenter of the 1929 earthquake
It required numerous submarine expeditions to observe the Earth's core
It began after she herself felt the Murchison earthquake in 1929
It was carried out from a country with no deep ocean or active volcano
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The card stresses that Lehmann worked from Denmark, a country with no deep ocean or active volcano, relying on nothing but the traces of a seismograph rather than direct observation.
